common_name: White Chiffon Rose of Sharon (Sterile Double-Flowered White Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; as a sterile triploid, White Chiffon sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance of older rose of sharon.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood, since bloom occurs on new growth. White Chiffon bears large, semi-double, pure white flowers with a soft, ruffled cluster of extra petals at the center that gives each bloom a fuller, more anemone-like look than the typical single rose of sharon flower, blooming from midsummer into fall. As a sterile selection, it produces almost no seed, sidestepping the self-sowing weediness that has given older rose of sharon a mixed reputation, while still delivering months of clean white color from a tough, low-maintenance shrub. It tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established.

common_name: Lavender Chiffon Rose of Sharon (Sterile Double-Flowered Lavender Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; as a sterile triploid, Lavender Chiffon sets little to no seed.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Lavender Chiffon bears large, soft lavender-blue flowers with a ruffled cluster of extra petaloids at the center that gives the bloom a fuller, semi-double appearance, opening from midsummer into fall on a tough, reliable, low-maintenance shrub. Like the other Chiffon-series rose of sharon, it is a sterile triploid, setting almost no seed and avoiding the volunteer-seedling problem common in older rose of sharon plantings. Its soft, cool flower color pairs well with warmer-toned summer perennials, and it tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil with ease once established.

common_name: Sugar Tip Rose of Sharon (Variegated Sterile Pink Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; variegation is brightest with several hours of direct sun.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Sugar Tip stands apart from other rose of sharon cultivars for its striking blue-green foliage crisply edged in creamy white, providing ornamental interest even before the double, soft pink flowers open from midsummer into fall. As a sterile selection, it sets little to no seed, avoiding the self-sowing weediness of older rose of sharon while adding season-long variegated foliage color that few other rose of sharon cultivars offer. It tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established, making it a low-maintenance, multi-season shrub for a sunny border.

common_name: Blue Satin Rose of Sharon (Azurri Blue Satin, Large Blue-Purple Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Blue Satin bears some of the largest flowers of any rose of sharon cultivar, single blooms up to 5 inches across in a rich blue-purple with a small red eye at the center, opening from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, well-branched shrub. Its bold flower size and saturated color make it a strong summer focal point in a mixed border or informal hedge, and like other modern rose of sharon selections it sets relatively little seed compared to old-fashioned, seed-grown althea. It tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established, needing little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning.

common_name: Purple Pillar Rose of Sharon (Columnar Narrow-Growing Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the narrow columnar habit fits tight side-yard beds and narrow spaces where a spreading shrub would not fit.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants closely to form a narrow, upright screen or leave as a single columnar accent. Purple Pillar is a distinctively narrow, columnar rose of sharon that grows as tall as the species while staying only 2–3 feet wide, an unusually upright form that fits tight side-yard beds, narrow entry plantings, and vertical accents where a normal spreading rose of sharon would not fit. It produces the same double, rich purple-violet flowers as other modern rose of sharon cultivars from midsummer into fall, on a shrub whose narrow silhouette makes it useful for privacy screening in a limited footprint. Prune in late winter to maintain the columnar form and encourage vigorous new flowering wood.

common_name: Aphrodite Rose of Sharon (Deep Pink Red-Eyed Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Bred by the US National Arboretum, Aphrodite bears large, single, deep rose-pink flowers with a prominent dark red eye at the center, a bold, saturated color combination that reads clearly from a distance, blooming heavily from midsummer into fall. It is a sterile or nearly sterile triploid selection, setting little seed compared to old-fashioned rose of sharon and avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance common with seed-grown plants, while remaining a tough, heat- and humidity-tolerant shrub. It requires little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and encourage the current season's flowering wood.

common_name: Miss Ruby Butterfly Bush (Sterile Rose-Pink Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to about 12 inches to encourage vigorous new flowering growth.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard to about 12 inches in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth. Miss Ruby is a North Carolina State University-bred sterile butterfly bush, producing dense, conical spikes of vivid rose-pink to magenta-red flowers continuously from summer through frost, with minimal deadheading needed since it sets almost no viable seed. Its more compact, well-behaved habit compared to older Buddleja davidii selections fits smaller borders while still delivering the heavy butterfly and hummingbird traffic the genus is known for. It tolerates heat and drought well once its root system is established, needing little care beyond the annual hard cutback.
sources: North Carolina State University JC Raulston Arboretum

common_name: Blue Chip Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Sterile Compact Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new flowering growth.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth. Blue Chip was one of the first true dwarf butterfly bush cultivars introduced, staying under 3 feet tall and wide — a fraction of the size of older Buddleja davidii selections — while still producing lavender-blue flower spikes continuously from summer through frost. Its compact, mounding, sterile habit fits containers, small borders, and mass plantings where full-size butterfly bush would need constant hard pruning to control, and it draws butterflies and hummingbirds heavily despite its small stature. It tolerates heat and drought well once established, needing little care beyond the annual cutback.
sources: North Carolina State University JC Raulston Arboretum

common_name: Longwood Purple American Wisteria (Non-Invasive Native Wisteria Selection)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring near a very strong support; unlike seed-grown American wisteria, named cultivars like Longwood Purple bloom reliably from a young age.

directions: Plant near a very strong trellis, pergola, or fence in full sun to partial shade; unlike the invasive Asian wisterias, this native selection is well-behaved and will not escape into natural areas. Longwood Purple, selected at Longwood Gardens, is a vigorous, heavy-blooming American wisteria cultivar with dense, fragrant, blue-purple flower clusters in late spring and good repeat bloom through summer, a reliability that seed-grown American wisteria does not consistently offer. It flowers at a younger age than seed-grown plants and responds well to pruning, staying more manageable than the aggressive Chinese and Japanese wisteria species widely sold. Prune twice yearly — once after the main spring bloom and again in late winter — to maintain size and encourage flowering spurs.

common_name: Victorian Lady Abutilon (Ruffled Pink Flowering Maple)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade. Victorian Lady bears large, ruffled, bell-shaped flowers in soft pink with darker pink veining, hanging gracefully from a tall, upright, well-branched shrub with maple-shaped leaves, blooming nearly year-round in mild climates. Its old-fashioned, cottage-garden charm and long bloom season make it a favorite for mixed borders and large containers where its upright habit fits better than trailing abutilon types, and hummingbirds visit the pendant flowers regularly. In zone 8, expect frost dieback most winters, with plants often resprouting from the base if roots are mulched and protected; where hard freezes are common, grow it in a container that can be moved to shelter for winter.

common_name: Nabob Abutilon (Deep Red Classic Flowering Maple)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade. Nabob is a longtime classic abutilon cultivar valued for its deep, velvety burgundy-red, bell-shaped flowers held against dark green, maple-shaped leaves, blooming nearly year-round in mild climates on an upright, well-branched shrub. Its rich, saturated flower color stands out among the typically softer pastel tones of many abutilon cultivars, making it a strong accent in mixed borders and large containers, and hummingbirds visit the pendant blooms regularly. In zone 8, expect frost dieback most winters, with plants often resprouting from the base if roots are mulched and protected; where hard freezes are common, grow it in a container that can be moved to shelter for winter.
